title.narrative: Strengthening Civil society for Older people's Rights and Engagement

description.narrative:
Challenges and Solutions 1. Pace of Project Implementation: The Project Implementation pace has been very fast with overlapping of multiple tasks within the first 5 months (August – December 2025). This had been a challenge because funds were only disbursed in October 2025, leaving only 5 months to conclude the 8 months plan. Solution: Although HAM has replanned the activities to be spread across November 2025 to March 2026, with realistic timelines, timely implementation of activities remained a challenge during the reporting period. Nevertheless, HAM delivered on all its outputs.
2. Project personnel to lead the project: The granting of the project to HAM coincided with the beginning of the localisation process. HAM is in the initial phase of its existence as a localised national NGO. Although it inherited the HelpAge International staff members and systems, the new setup has a different governance and operational structure and is in its lower side of the learning curve. Solution: To address this challenge the HAM Executive Director took lead of the programme coordination with the assistance of Monitoring and Evaluation Officer, until a Project Officer for SCORE is recruited. The delay in recruiting the Project Officer is as fully explained above, under Outcome 1.
3. Finance Management: HAM as a new entity, had to establish its own Professional Accounting system. Attempt were made to acquire and use QUIKBOOKS, however, this did not materialise for lack of technical expertise and support of this software in the country. In the absence of a Professional Accounting Package, HAM managed its accounts on Excel. To mitigate challenges imposed by this, monthly budget monitoring meetings were held where all the accounts, including individual transactions were analysed, discussed and approved. The technical capacity of the Finance Manager in managing the transition was another challenge. The lack of support staff in Finance and Administration was identified as the main contributory factor, to the low efficiency of the Finance Manager. Solution: HAM does not have enough funds to employ an additional personnel member in Finance and Administration, hence capacity strengthening of the current Finance Manager is the feasible solution being pursued. The acquisition and operationalisation of a renowned PRIMAVERA Accounting package was only completed in March 2026. The SCORE Project partially contributed to this investment. 4. Anchoring HAM Proposals: Experience over the past year has shown that HAM as a young organization cannot successfully win the trust of external donors on its own. Although some quality proposals were developed and submitted during this year, none of them were funded. One of the potential donors expressed worry over HAM’s capacity to implement, given its young age. Solution: In this respect, the continuous presence of HAI as an anchor of HAM proposals to external donors will be of great assistance together with the journey of capacity strengthening that the organization is implementing via the OIP. 5. Compliance: HAM inherited compliance structures from HAI. However, the systems that hold together compliance, such as Accounting and Procurement packages (software) were not inherited. Solution: Capacity strengthening of HAM’s stand-alone Finance systems is an area where HAI support via the due diligence and OIP processes would make a substantial difference 6. Due Diligence: The Due Diligence process was challenging due to the organisation’s early stage of institutional development and ongoing localisation journey. Multiple rounds of document review and clarification were required, particularly around governance structures, internal policies, financial controls, and compliance systems. Solution: To address this, the organisation developed and strengthened key institutional policies, improved documentation practices, and established an institutional capacity strengthening plan to meet donor compliance requirements while building sustainable national leadership. 7. Floods: Mozambique experienced the worst floods over the past 20 years, affecting all the 3 Provinces where HAM has its field operations. In all the 3 Provinces Older people were seriously affected, and some projects such as Income generation Activities supported by HAM with other funding sources were washed away by the floods. HAM had to mobilise and provide a response to the natural disaster. The drafting of the response and delivery of assistance seriously overstretched the implementation capacity of HAM programme and operations staff. This affected the expediency of HAM business with partners including SCORE Programme. Solution: To address this challenge, remote working was promoted and implemented to allow business continuity. In the medium term, funding allowing, special personnel would have to be deployed to address any humanitarian situation.

Locally anchored civil society effectively challenges ageism, amplifies the voices, and protects the rights, of older people in all their diversities to take action to reduce poverty at national, regional, and global levels.

MEAL During the reporting period, the SCORE Programme operationalised a structured Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) system to support timely and reliable data collection, strengthen accountability, and ensure that older people’s voices inform programme decision-making and adaptation. MEAL system structure and responsibilities The MEAL system is implemented through a decentralised structure involving the MEAL Officer, Programme Manager, field facilitators, and implementing partner staff. Roles are clearly assigned as follows: • Community-level data collection: Field facilitators and Older People’s Associations (OPAs) collect routine monitoring data on participation, service delivery, and community activities. • Partner-level reporting: Anchor CSOs compile monthly implementation data using standardised tools and submit reports through the Digital MEAL System (DMS). • MEAL unit oversight: The MEAL Officer validates, consolidates, analyses, and quality-assures data before reporting. Data collection tools and frequency A standardised set of tools is used across SCORE implementation sites to ensure consistency and comparability of data: • Monthly activity monitoring tools: Track implementation progress and participation in programme activities. • Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) tools: Assess relevance, satisfaction, and outcomes after humanitarian or livelihood support interventions. • Pre- and post-training assessment tools: Measure knowledge and skills acquired through capacity-strengthening activities. • Organisational Capacity Assessment Tool (OCAT): Applied annually to measure institutional strengthening among Anchor CSOs. • Community feedback and CRM tools: Continuously capture feedback, complaints, and suggestions from older people. Routine monitoring data is collected monthly; training and distribution data is collected by activity cycle; and organisational assessment data is collected annually through the OCAT. Accountability to older people and feedback mechanisms The SCORE Programme has established community-based accountability mechanisms to ensure that older people’s voices are systematically captured and used to improve programme implementation. These mechanisms include: • Community Feedback Mechanisms (CRM): Structured channels for older people to provide feedback, suggestions, and complaints on programme implementation. • Older People’s Associations (OPAs): Primary platforms for collective voice, enabling older people to raise community-level concerns and escalate them to programme staff. • Community dialogue sessions: Periodic meetings between programme teams, OPAs, and community members to review progress and discuss challenges. Although formal grievance reporting remained limited during the reporting period, qualitative feedback collected through OPAs and community dialogues was actively used to adjust targeting, improve service delivery, and refine implementation approaches. Integrating older people’s voices into programme adaptation Feedback collected through OPAs, community dialogues, and CRM mechanisms is reviewed during monthly programme meetings. Key issues raised by older people are documented in MEAL reports and incorporated into implementation adjustments, particularly around the targeting of vulnerable households, accessibility of services, and timing of activities. This feedback loop helps ensure that programme adaptation is both data-driven and grounded in the lived experiences and priorities of older people. Data quality assurance and validation To strengthen reliability and accuracy, the programme applies the following data quality assurance measures: • Routine data verification checks during monthly reporting cycles. • Cross-validation of partner reports against field-level records and attendance registers. • Use of standardised reporting templates within the Digital MEAL System (DMS) to reduce inconsistencies. • Regular feedback sessions with implementing partners to address reporting gaps and improve data consistency.
MEAL capacity strengthening and alignment During the reporting period, the MEAL Officer participated in a structured capacity-strengthening and alignment process focused on finalising and operationalising country-level MEAL systems and tools under the SCORE Programme. This process was grounded in the global SCORE Results Framework and helped align country-level indicators, reporting tools, and data systems with donor requirements and programme objectives. Baseline development and framework alignment A structured baseline process was initiated using Organisational Capacity Assessment (OCA/OCAT) results, programme inception data, and partner reporting reviews. The OCAT baseline established an initial organisational capacity score of 36%, which serves as the reference point for tracking institutional strengthening under Indicator 1.1.1.2. This baseline has been used to define incremental annual targets toward the programme endline target of a 30% overall increase in organisational capacity. Baseline data for outcome-level indicators, particularly Outcome 3 on empowerment and accountability, was also consolidated through a review of existing programme data and community-level verification exercises. The country-specific MEAL framework and implementation plan are being adapted from the global SCORE MEAL framework and are scheduled for finalisation in Year 2 to ensure full contextual alignment. MEAL systems strengthening and tools operationalisation Capacity-strengthening sessions supported country teams to finalise results frameworks, assign reporting responsibilities, and populate baseline and target values across all indicators. Teams were also trained on Detailed Implementation Plans (DIPs), MEAL calendars, and the Digital MEAL System (DMS), improving the standardisation of data entry, disaggregation, and reporting processes. MEAL practices implemented during the reporting period The following MEAL practices were introduced or strengthened during the reporting period: • Post-distribution monitoring (PDM): PDM exercises were conducted in programme areas affected by shocks, providing real-time feedback on service delivery quality and beneficiary satisfaction. Findings informed adjustments to targeting and support modalities for older people. • Complaints and feedback mechanisms: Community feedback mechanisms were operationalised to capture grievances and suggestions from older people. Although formal grievance reporting remains limited, qualitative feedback has been systematically used to adjust field implementation approaches. • Routine monitoring and data quality checks: Monthly data verification and cross-checking exercises were introduced to strengthen data reliability and improve reporting consistency across implementing partners. Key results and use of MEAL data MEAL data collected during the reporting period contributed directly to programme adaptation and decision-making. Key examples include: • Organisational capacity: OCAT results confirmed a 40% improvement in organisational capacity scores, exceeding planned targets for the reporting period. • Empowerment and accountability: Outcome monitoring showed that 61.7% of older people reported increased knowledge and confidence to claim their rights, indicating positive progress toward empowerment objectives. Training effectiveness: Training assessments demonstrated measurable improvement in participant knowledge following capacity-building sessions.Cross cutting issues:

Older people's voices are heard, and rights better upheld through a thriving, inclusive and locally anchored civil society advocating with and for them. This will lead to less multi-dimensional poverty and age-based discrimination experienced by older people.

Outcome 1: Locally anchored national civil society organisations have strengthened capacity to act strategically with and on behalf of older people Activity 1.1 Capacity strengthening initiative During the reporting period 6 HAM staff (4 men and 2 women) participated to the following capacity strengthening trainings: • Project Launch Meeting Sessions 1 and 2 including financial and compliance management on 15 and 16 October 2025. The meeting provided a clear introduction to the SCORE Programme’s objectives and implementation strategy. It also covered key compliance requirements, with a focus on financial management and overall programme management. • Environmental Assessment on 23 October 2025. The training focused on integrating environmental considerations into programme planning and implementation. It emphasised the need to ensure that SCORE activities avoid environmental degradation and minimise the programme’s carbon footprint wherever possible. • Capacity Strengthening Focal Points Induction on 21 October 2025. The induction provided detailed guidance on SCORE Programme management, including the role of the Focal Person, communication lines, information flow, and reporting timelines. • Anti-bribery, fraud and corruption on 11 November 2025. The training was mandatory for all individuals involved in implementing the SCORE Programme. It reinforced the programme’s zero-tolerance approach to corruption and corrupt practices, emphasising the obligation to report any suspected corruption. This obligation also applies to suppliers. • Safeguarding training on 13 November 2025. The safeguarding training focused on preventing harm to older people, children, women and persons with disabilities during programme implementation. It strengthened staff capacity to identify safeguarding risks, understand appropriate reporting pathways, and report any suspected violations in a timely and responsible manner. • Data protection training on 26 November 2025: The training highlighted the importance of protecting SCORE Programme data and reinforced staff responsibilities for handling information securely, responsibly and in line with data protection requirements. • Security training Sessions – 14 January 2026 and 2 February 2026. The training focused on staff safety during programme implementation, with particular attention to teams working in high-risk areas. Participants were reminded to follow established security protocols, including those used by large organisations such as the United Nations. The training reinforced that staff safety remains a core principle across all programme activities. • IATI training on 20 October 2025. The training focused on publishing information from SCORE Project partners on the IATI platform. It reinforced the importance of transparent reporting and compliance with programme and donor requirements.
During the reporting period, the focal point lead has been the Executive Director assisted by the Monitoring Evaluation and Learning Officer. The recruitment of a Project Officer was initiated in February 2026 and would conclude in the next Quarter. Once recruited, the Project Officer will take over as the lead CS focal point. The following table summarises the focal Point arrangements for the first year of SCORE:
Post % Time share Executive Director 50% Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning Officer 50% Finance Manager 60% Logistics Assistant 49%
The recruitment of the Project Officer to lead coordination of SCORE Project, has been delayed because of the Labour Law requirement prohibiting recruitment of a replacement position within 60 days after termination of a contract of a previous post-holder which in this case ended in December 2025. Therefore, the recruitment of the Project Officer could only start in February 2026, to comply with the law. Breach of this provision may expose HAM to legal suit by the previous post holder. Activity 1.1.1 Capacity assessment workshops In preparation of the Organizational Capacity Assessment (OCA) workshop HAM staff participated to an orientation session on OCA guidelines conducted by HelpAge International capacity strengthening consultant where the tools and purpose of the exercise was clarified. Furthermore, a capacity strengthening methods workshop was organized on 9 December where SCORE partners had more detailed guidelines on how to translate the gaps identified in the OCA with tangible and practical actions that will lead to an improved organization that goes beyond the simple training or hiring of a consultant. Furthermore, on 15th December HAM had the opportunity to discuss with HAI Capacity Strengthening Manager and the Capacity Strengthening consultant the structure of its OCA and request any tips or support to design the sessions. Originally a member of the Global SCORE team was supposed to join HAM in its OCA but due to visa delays it was not possible. During the reporting period, HelpAge Mozambique conducted a three-day Organizational Capacity Assessment (OCA) workshop between 16 and 19 December 2025, engaging 12 participants (6 women and 6 men) from senior management, programme, finance, MEAL, administrative staff, and partner organizations. The assessment was conducted using the Save the Children OCA tool for CSOs, which provided a robust, structured, and participatory framework to systematically assess organisational strengths and gaps across key functional areas. The only adaptation provided was the translation in Portuguese. The use of this tool enabled evidence-based analysis strengthened internal reflection and alignment among teams, and informed the identification of clear, prioritised actions for organisational capacity strengthening, contributing to more effective, accountable, and sustainable programme delivery. The workshop employed a structured, participatory methodology, combining self-assessment exercises, facilitated group discussions, and interactive reflection sessions to evaluate organisational strengths and gaps. Participants identified key areas for improvement, including human resources systems, governance, financial management, and monitoring and evaluation, while recognising strong staff commitment and mission clarity. The workshop was facilitated by an external consultant, a renowned Organisation Development Specialist. The workshop fostered alignment across teams and a shared understanding of institutional challenges, enabling participants to collaboratively develop a practical organisation improvement plan (OIP). This plan establishes measurable priorities and will guide HelpAge Mozambique’s organisational strengthening efforts throughout SCORE Programme period and beyond, ensuring that interventions are targeted, sustainable, and responsive to the evolving needs of the organization and its partner OPAs. Activity 1.1.2 Implementation of the Organisational Strengthening Plan Following the OCA prioritisation process, HAM developed and began implementing an Organisational Improvement Plan covering the first year until March 2026 to address the key institutional gaps identified. Professional consultants were engaged to support the drafting and finalisation of essential operational documents and guidelines such as: Strategic Plan finalised, enabling its operationalisation. • Board Governance Manual drafted. • Finance and Administration Manual drafted. • Human Resources Management Manual drafted. • Procurement and Internal Controls Manual drafted. • Strategic Plan finalised, enabling its operationalisation. HAM has completed the final draft of its Strategic Plan, which is pending Board approval before it is shared with network partners and rolled out. All other draft documents have also been submitted for formal endorsement by the Board. The OCA also identified migration to a professional accounting system as a priority for strengthening finance management. The SCORE Programme partially funded the acquisition of the accounting system (Primavera) and related user training, supporting improved financial controls, reporting and accountability. The OIP also identified the need to develop and implement additional organisational policies to strengthen institutional systems, accountability and programme quality. The priority policies include: • Gender Policy; • Safeguarding Policy; and • Green Office Policy. The drafting and implementation of these policies, together with any additional policies identified during the process, will be carried forward under the Year 2 Organisational Improvement Plan. During the reporting period HAM staff participated to a training organized by Capacity Strengthening Manager about leading Organisation Change. The training focused on how SCORE local leadership and teams can engineer the Organisation Development of the Anchor CSO to become efficient and effective in programme delivery beyond the SCORE Programme Cycle.
Activity 1.1.4 SCORE in-person capacity building workshop (Ethiopia) During Year 1, 2 HAM Staff members took part in an in-person workshop organized by HelpAge International in Ethiopia between 19 and 24 January 2026, that brought together 8 Anchor CSOs of SCORE. The six-day training delivered a comprehensive and high-impact capacity strengthening experience, combining strategic alignment, technical learning, and practical application. It began by reinforcing a shared understanding of the SCORE programme’s objectives, compliance requirements, and coordination mechanisms, ensuring stronger coherence and accountability across teams. Through peer learning and exchange, participants critically reflected on the organisational capacity assessments, identified priority areas for institutional strengthening, and fostered collaboration across countries. The training significantly strengthened competencies in planning and MEAL, with a strong focus on results-based management, indicators, data quality, and evidence-driven decision-making. Cross-cutting areas such as communication, ethical storytelling, branding, and visibility enhanced participants’ ability to effectively demonstrate impact and engage stakeholders. Dedicated sessions on gender and inclusion deepened understanding of intersectionality and supported the practical integration of inclusive approaches across programme cycles. The inclusion of team-building activities further strengthened trust and collaboration within the network. The training concluded with practical field exposure and targeted sessions on resource mobilisation, equipping participants with concrete tools—such as the POP (Problem, Opportunity, Proposal) framework—to develop compelling proposals and strengthen engagement with donors. Overall, the training strengthened both individual and organisational capacities, positioning partners to deliver more effective, inclusive, and sustainable interventions under the SCORE programme. HAM learned from the other network members key issues that would feed back into its programme: • Networking and Advocacy: The implementation of the UHC Toolkit taught HAM that through Networking is possible to undertake an impactful advocacy. • Intergenerational programming: A deliberate policy is being undertaken by some Anchor CSOs in ensuring that young people are included in the activities undertaken by Older Peoples Associations. For HAM, this is a key learning to be included in its programming. • Organisation Policies: HAM is in the process of drafting its organisation policies and has learned that some of the Anchor CSOs present at the workshop have all the necessary policies in place and that they are willing to share them as example for learning purposes. HAM does not need to re-invent the wheel but will adapt some of the policies that have already been developed by the others. • Strengthening MEAL Systems: The workshop reinforced the importance of having clear indicators, structured data collection processes, and systematic learning loops. HAM gained practical insights on how other members operationalise their MEAL systems to inform decision-making and improve programme quality. • Participatory Grant-Making Approaches: Exposure to participatory grant-making principles highlighted the value of transparency, accountability, and partner ownership in grants management. HAM will explore ways to strengthen inclusive decision-making processes in its partnership management. • Institutional Communication and Storytelling: Sessions on branding, ethical content collection, and storytelling emphasised the importance of demonstrating impact through clear, consistent narratives. HAM will strengthen its communication practices to better align programme results with donor engagement and advocacy objectives. Overall, the workshop strengthened HAM’s strategic outlook, enhanced institutional learning, and reinforced its commitment to continuous improvement through peer exchange and network collaboration. Activity 1.1.5 Age, Gender and Inclusion assessment preparation On 26 November 2025, HelpAge Mozambique participated in an online meeting on gender, age and inclusion analysis/assessment, facilitated by HelpAge International’s Gender and Inclusion Advisor. This initial orientation session was designed as a preparatory step for the in-person training scheduled for January 2026 and aimed to better understand the organisation’s current approaches, needs, and capacity gaps related to gender and inclusion mainstreaming within programme implementation. The discussion focused on reviewing existing approaches to gender mainstreaming, age inclusion, and broader inclusive programming practices across the programme cycle, including design, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and advocacy. Particular attention was given to the team’s experience and confidence in the collection, use, and analysis of Sex, Age and Disability Disaggregated Data (SADDD), as well as the tools, frameworks, and guidelines currently in use to support gender-sensitive and inclusive programming. The meeting also provided space to identify key operational gaps and challenges, including areas where staff required additional technical support to strengthen inclusive and targeted interventions, especially for older women, older men, and persons with disabilities. In parallel, the discussion explored contextual opportunities for strengthening gender-transformative and inclusive approaches, as well as priority training needs to inform the design of a more tailored and practical training session for the January workshop. A key outcome of the meeting was the identification of priority capacity-strengthening areas, particularly around mainstreaming gender and inclusion across all stages of programming, strengthening the use of disaggregated data for evidence-based decision-making, and developing strategies to cascade learning across wider programme teams. As a follow-up to this meeting, Terms of Reference were drafted for an engagement of a consultant to lead the contextual analysis of Gender, Age and Inclusion in Mozambique. A consultant was recruited on a competitive process and conducted the assessment which used two complementary methods: desk research based on secondary data, and key informant interviews with major groups of interest. This approach provided both documentary evidence and stakeholder perspectives to inform the analysis. A total of 32 documents were reviewed, including relevant legislation on the protection of older people, social protection, gender, disability and related areas. The review also covered public policies and national strategies on gender equality, social action, basic social security, ageing, inclusion and the protection of vulnerable groups, as well as reports, evaluations, studies and policy briefs that helped identify gaps between the regulatory framework and its practical implementation. The consultants interviewed representatives from relevant institutions, including the Ministry of Gender and Social Welfare, the National Statistics Office, the United Nations Population Fund, UN Women, and executive members of the Gender Coalition Network, among others. In total, 17 people were consulted, including 10 women and 7 men. The HAI Gender and Age Inclusion Advisor supported the process by reviewing the Terms of Reference and guiding the HAM team in following up on the consultancy work. The preliminary findings were discussed with HAM programme staff before the final report was issued in Portuguese, this will be translated in English and shared in the second year of the programme. The assessment report has been adopted as a primary reference for mainstreaming gender, age and inclusion across the Programme. Full details of the report’s major findings are presented in the Cross-Cutting Issues section below.
Activity 1.2 Core funding for anchor national entities In line with the partner contract funding agreement between HelpAge International and HelpAge Mozambique, the organization utilized part of the SOS funding provided by HelpAge International as co funding for the SCORE Programme for a total of GBP 23,333 during the first year of the SCORE Programme. HelpAge Mozambique met this commitment by allocating resources across key operational and support cost areas. These contributions were recorded across different months during the reporting period and are summarized as follows: • Support staff costs including medical expenses: A total of GBP 15,264.54 was contributed through proportional salary allocations for support staff • Office running costs: GBP 6.510.37 was covered for essential office expenses, including office rent, internet, electricity, cleaning, stationary, water, coffee and communication costs, all of which directly linked to SCORE co-funding. This includes expenses related to the Board Meetings. • Vehicle running costs: GBP 933.03 was allocated for fuel, vehicle servicing, and maintenance to support programme activities. • Complementary activities of the OIP: HAM acquired QuickBooks Accounting package, through SOS funds. A Consultant was hired to conduct a technical assessment of operationability of QuickBooks (GBP 238,88). However, after thorough review, it was concluded that it would be difficult to work on QuickBooks Accounting package because it lacked specialist technical expertise support in the country. A decision was made to do migration to PRIMAVERA Accounting package. The SOS through SCORE Programme contributed for webhosting of the PRIMAVERA Accounting Operating System (GBP 386.85) and for technical assessment of the PRIMAVERA Accounting package vis-a-vis QuikBooks for a total of GBP 625.06

Outcome 2: Civil society have a stronger voice and opportunities for dialogue and collaboration with diverse stakeholders that are more engaged in ageing issues
During the International Day of the Older Person (1st October), HAM was actively involved in high level national events advocating for the issues of older people. The HAM Executive Director and Board Chair took part in 6 National TV Programmes in panel discussions and interviews on ageing issues. The media events amplified HAM’s message advocating for the implementation of universal social protection for older people.
Activity 2.1 Project grants to CSOs for engagement with government and stakeholders to build momentum and broad support for action on ageing issues
During the reporting period, 2 consultation sessions were conducted on participatory grants mechanism with the Anchor CSOs on 18 and 27 of November together with a detailed survey with guiding questions on how to create the participatory mechanism. HAM Project Team was empowered with their contribution on how the grant mechanism would function and a process document including ToR of the Steering and Grant Management Committee has been created in a participatory manner. This document included selection criteria for both committee members and in December 2025 based on these guidelines HAM selected: • For Steering Committee: Rosália Verónica Vasco Mutisse who is the Board Chari of HelpAge Mozambique based on her three decades of work experience in development sector with focus on Project Management. • For Grants Management Committee: Simao Hodges Chatepa who is the Executive Director of HelpAge Mozambique based on his bast experience in NGO and Development sector including assisting civil society organizations in drafting funding proposals.
During the in-person workshop held in Ethiopia in January 2026, the HAM Executive Director and MEAL Officer participated in discussions on the Participatory Grant Mechanism. The sessions focused on defining the focus areas for both Large and Small Grants, clarifying eligibility criteria, and agreeing on the process for proposal evaluation. The It was agreed that proposals should contribute to at least one of SCORE’s thematic priorities: • Income security, including social protection; • Climate resilience, including adaptation and disaster risk reduction; and • Human rights, voice and ageism. • Healthy ageing, including universal health coverage. At the end of January 2026, the large grant call for proposal was launched and all anchor CSOs were confirmed as eligible to apply. Further guidance on eligibility requirements and application procedures was provided through drop-in sessions held on 4 February 2026. The Grants Management Committee reviewed all proposals and confirmed the successful applicants which after validations of the Steering Committee were invited to review their budget and proposals based on the GMC comments. HAM submitted one proposal under Outcome 2 which was successful, and following rounds of review funding was allocated for implementation in Year 2. The HAM project will strengthen networks of organisations working on older people’s rights so they can engage authorities on key policy issues more effectively. It will also expand ageing-related advocacy and programme implementation to Nampula Province in northern Mozambique, one of the country’s most populous regions and an area where older people’s rights remain insufficiently fulfilled.
Activity 2.2 Global and regional level engagement to generate opportunities for dialogue and collaboration to deliver change at the national level
Activity not undertaken during the reporting period.
Activity 2.3 Initiatives, tools, and analysis to strengthen CSOs for national and regional advocacy
Activity 2.3.1 Pilot training on Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Voice Toolkit Pilot
Organisation and Participation: In October 2025, HAM attended an orientation provided by HAI UHC consultant which outlined the timeline and deliverables expected under this activity. The Mozambican government has a comprehensive UHC strategy based on Primary Health Care and HelpAge Mozambique plans to support the Ministry of Health amplifying its message. During the reporting period HAM conducted a four days’ workshop between 9 and 12 December 2025 with the aim to strengthen the capacities of older people and partner organizations to understand, advocate for, and promote the right to health and Universal Health Coverage (UHC), with particular attention to the specific needs of older people.
The training brought together a total of 33 participants, reflecting a diverse and inclusive group composition. This included 23 older people (approximately 70% of participants) from 12 communities in Manhiça District—Dzonguene, Maguiguana, Eduardo Mondlane, 3 de Fevereiro, Nhamatibjana, Malavele, Círculo Ribangua, Círculo Mulembja, Maciana, Maluana, Círculo Tsa-Tse, and Círculo Cambeve. Their participation ensured that the training was grounded in community-level realities and lived experiences of older persons across different local contexts. The remaining 10 participants represented key institutional stakeholders, including civil society and government actors, including2 participants from ACIDECO (a local association), 3 representatives from HelpAge Mozambique, 3 representatives from the District Social Welfare Office, and 1 consultant supported by 1 assistant. The diverse participation strengthened multi-stakeholder engagement, promoting dialogue and collaboration between community members, service providers, and implementing partners.
In terms of gender distribution, the training had a strong female representation, with 21 women (64%) and 12 men (36%), which is particularly relevant given the vulnerabilities and active roles of older women in community structures. The age distribution also reflected intergenerational participation: 30% of participants were aged between 30 and 50 years, 34% between 51 and 65 years, and 36% were above 65 years, some as old as 80 years. This diversity allowed for meaningful exchange between younger professionals and older community members, enriching discussions with both technical perspectives and lived experiences.
Overall, the composition of participants contributed to a balanced, inclusive, and contextually relevant learning environment, enhancing both the quality of discussions and the applicability of the training outcomes.
Focus and Takeaways: The main focus was on access to health services by older people under the Universal Health Coverage Declaration from WHO, to which Mozambique is a signatory. As a result of the capacity strengthening, the members drafted a Petition calling for improved access to public health services by older people. The petition was submitted to the Manhiça District Health Department and received by the District Director who made a commitment to address the issues. In addition to the drafting and submission of the Petition, the capacity strengthening resulted in the following key take aways:
Skills in Evidence Based Advocacy: The workshop focuses on identifying real life issues that need be addressed and enabled the participants to understand how evidence-based advocacy works.
Pro-active Empowering: The participants were empowered with being pro-active in the issues affecting them. The workshop methodology demanded that the participants actively participate and contribute to the discussion. By the end of the day, participants recognised that the final draft petition was built from their own contributions. This realisation highlighted that, by being proactive, they can address the issues affecting them in a timely manner, rather than waiting for others to take the lead.
Understanding the Power Dynamics and effect on the fulfilment of Older Person Rights: The workshop enabled participants to analyse the power dynamics within their respective communities and environments, and how these influence the realisation of the rights of older people. For instance, participants identified that decision-making on the delivery of quality health services for older people largely rests with the District Health Department. As a result, they strategically directed their petition to this key government institution.
Participants Feedback: Participants’ main feedback highlighted that they experienced the process as highly empowering. Through the workshop, they strengthened their knowledge and skills in advocacy. Most importantly, they realised that by acting collectively, they have the ability to influence change in their own interests. The drafting and submission of the petition was seen as a particularly empowering experience. As expressed by one participant, Ms Isaura Deve (74, Manhiça, 12 December 2025): ‘For the first time in our lives, we have submitted a petition to the Government.’”
Follow-up action: The follow-up action planned in the previous reporting period was conducted on 30–31 March 2026 in Maluana. The exercise aimed to assess progress on issues raised in the petition submitted by older people regarding access to health services and to collect direct feedback from older people and health stakeholders.
The follow-up was implemented through two complementary approaches. First, community consultations and household visits were conducted with older people to gather feedback on their experiences accessing health services and to assess whether any improvements had been observed since the petition was submitted. The follow-up was led by 30 members (18 women and 12 men) of Maluana Older People Association (OPA) which managed to reach 536 community members (278 women and 258 men). Of these, 27 were older people (21 women and 6 men). Feedback remained largely negative, with older people reporting long waiting times, continued out-of-pocket payments for some prescribed medicines, shortages of age-appropriate medication, and concerns regarding the attitude and responsiveness of some health personnel.
Second, a dialogue meeting was held with approximately 50 participants, 30 women and 20 men (including older people) from four neighbourhoods, representatives of the Older People’s Association (OPA), and a representative of the Maluana Health Facility. Although the Health Facility Director was unable to attend, a delegated health technician participated and engaged directly with older people regarding the concerns raised in the petition.older people from four neighbourhoods, representatives of the Older People’s Association (OPA), and a representative of the Maluana Health Facility. Although the Health Facility Director was unable to attend, a delegated health technician participated and engaged directly with older people regarding the concerns raised in the petition.
Considering the low funding available for the follow up activity HAM decided to leverage on activities from another project to be able to gather this information.
The follow-up process generated several important outcomes. Older People received both formal and informal feedback from health authorities regarding issues raised in the petition, creating a stronger channel of communication between service providers and the community. The consultations also reaffirmed key priorities requiring continued advocacy, including improved treatment of older people within health facilities, increased availability of medicines relevant to age-related conditions, strengthened outreach services for housebound older people, and enhanced capacity of health workers on ageing and older people’s rights. While the follow-up did not yet identify significant service delivery changes, it demonstrated increased engagement of older people in accountability processes and strengthened dialogue between the community and health service providers. Additional engagement with district-level health authorities remains necessary to review implementation progress, address outstanding challenges, and agree on concrete actions to improve access to health services for older people.

Outcome 3: Older people and organisations representing them are coordinated and active agents of change on holding duty bearers accountable on key priorities
Activity 3.1 Project grants for amplified voice and coordinated action on rights Following the preparatory work for the Participatory Grants Mechanism described under Outcome 2, in order to amplify advocacy for the rights of older people under the SCORE Programme, HAM closely participated in the launch of the Small Grants call for proposal. Following agreement among the eight participating Anchor CSOs, the GMC and the SC on the Terms of Reference, eligibility criteria, and thematic focus, a drop-in session was convened on 12 March 2026 to explain the overall process.
It was clarified that the Small Grants process would align with the same outcomes as the Large Grants process, with differences in grant value and implementation period. The maximum grant value was set at GBP 10,000, with an implementation period of six to nine months. Each Anchor CSO would issue the Request for Proposals in its respective country, using the modality most appropriate to its context. From the applications received, each Anchor CSO would pre-select a maximum of four proposals (2 per each outcome) for further evaluation by the Grants Management Committee. In Mozambique, HAM shared the Small Grants call by email with a pre-selected group of seven civil society organisations (CSOs). The CSOs were selected because of their active role in promoting the rights of older people in Mozambique and their demonstrated track record of work at community level. Three of the seven organisations are existing HAM partners under the Irish Aid-funded programme ROAR. Given the short application window, HAM limited the call to organisations with proven experience and tangible evidence of ongoing activities, helping to ensure a focused and timely application process.
After the launch, on 25 March 2026, HAM organized a drop-in session to explain the application process and respond to questions from potential applicants.
A local Grant Management Committee was formed in March 2026, composed of 2 HAM staff (Executive Director, male; MEAL Officer, female) and 2 Board members (Board Chair, female; Vice-Board Chair, female). HAM invited people as well from the Academia and other CSOs, however, the invited representatives were unable to participate due to the short timeframe for completing the process. Receipt and review of proposals will take place in Year 2 of the Programme.

recipient-country.narrative: The SCORE Programme is being implemented in Mozambique, a country where older people constitute 5% of the population meaning 1,678,620 Mozambicans out of 34,090,466, according to the Population and Housing Census Report (INE, 2025). From mid-December 2025 to end of February 2026, Mozambique experienced El Nina induced heavy rains resulting in severe flooding. The floods seriously affected three Southern Provinces of Gaza, Maputo and Inhambane in the South. A total of 1 million people were displaced by the floods and 184 lost their lives. In the centre part of the country, the floods severely affected Tete Province, coincidentally where HAM has field interventions too. With the assistance of HelpAge International Humanitarian Team, funding from Global Emergency Fund was secured to respond to the critical needs of Older People in Tete Province. A total of 210 Older Peoples households (with 2,087 persons) were directly people with Food and Non-Food Relief support. Older people in Mozambique face various challenges, the major ones being human rights abuse, neglect and inadequate social protection and legal framework. The Ministry of Labour, Gender and Social Welfare is responsible for any issue related to older people. However, this is one of the most underfunded Ministries according to the national budget allocation, receiving barely 2% of the state budget. HelpAge International Country Office in Mozambique finalised its localization process, that culminated with the creation of HelpAge Mozambique (HAM) as a national NGOs advocating for the rights of older people on 1st April 2025. A Board of Directors was established for the new entity, which also appointed its Executive Director. In addition to the staff, HelpAge Mozambique inherited equipment and well-established systems from HelpAge International which will continue providing technical support to HelpAge Mozambique for a period of three years after localisation. The SCORE Programme is an integral part of the Capacity Strengthening of HelpAge Mozambique in its new autonomous path. HAM is a leading local organisation promoting the rights of older people, building on the strong legacy and platform created by HelpAge International as a pioneer international NGO in this field. There are approximately 200 Civil Society Organisations (national NGOs, community-based organizations, older people associations) promoting and defending the rights of older people across the country. These organisations face various operational and structural challenges the major ones being the following: • Shallow networking: the organisations are working in very loose networks, hence unable to present an effective coordinated advocacy platform before the Authorities in defence of the rights of the older people. • Weak institutions: most organisations lack internal operational systems and working equipment and have inadequate resources and poorly trained personnel • Non-operational governance structures: most organisations’ governance structures are not functional hence posing a challenge to transparency and accountability of the internal business processes. Over the past year of SCORE Programme implementation, HelpAge Mozambique has focused on two key areas: • Strengthening its administrative and programme delivery capacities; and • Building stronger alliances to promote effective advocacy for the rights of older people in Mozambique. Regarding institutional capacity strengthening, all HAM staff participated in a range of capacity development initiatives delivered by the SCORE Project team and external specialists engaged specifically for this purpose. HAM was also successful in the Large Grants call for proposal launched under the SCORE Programme which will be an occasion to amplify HAM outreach to Nampula Province, one of the most vulnerable areas with respect to protection of the rights of older people. This will be an occasion to apply the strengthen programme delivery capacity. With respect to strengthening of alliances, HAM signed a 2-year Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Mozambican Ministry of Labour, Gender and Social Welfare, on 11 March 2026. The MOU would provide a strong forum of interaction for the advancement of the ageing issues. HelpAge Mozambique is in a privileged position, having inherited HelpAge International connections with the Government and being the only national Civil Society Organisations with a formal MoU with one of the Government Ministries. Furthermore, during the reporting period, HelpAge Mozambique actively engaged with two network organisations promoting the rights of older people: Forum da Terceira Idade (Older Age Forum) and Observatorio da Pessoa Idosa (Older People’s Observatory). These network organisations congregate at least 40 local associations across the country working for the rights of older people. The discussions with these organisations focused on several issues the main one being strengthening networking for effective advocacy for implementation of universal social protection and combating violence perpetrated against older persons.
